heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Background, 1.2 Our Work)
note: 10 blocks, 219 words, eight printed units. 21 opens on depletion of terrestrial minerals and the turn to space; 22 is the headline context number — “if asteroid 16 Psyche is successfully mined, each person on earth can share an average of 93 billion dollars” — which is background and is never used again in any model. 23 poses the three questions and glues “1.2 Our Work Figure 1: Our Work”. 24 is the work lead, and 25-30 are four bullet deliverables, each split by the line breaker into one or two blocks: build and validate an equity model (25), present one vision of the market and its impact (26-27), change conditions and analyse the effects (28), propose regulations (29-30). Each bullet names a product, so route throughout. Block 30's tail glues the section heading “Assumptions”. Front matter (Problem Chosen 1, title 2, Summary 3-9, keywords 10, table of contents 11-20) is not coded; the TOC in 11-20 is a dotted-leader dump that runs to “Page 3” inside block 19.

heading: 2 Assumptions
note: 13 measured blocks, 157 words, six bullets, every one cut into two or three line-fragments. Assumption 1 says asteroid resources are unlimited, which is assumed only “to make our discussion of long-round trend possible”; assumption 2 immediately says that at any moment the usable stock is “limited and scarce”, and defends that as the source of inequity. The pair is not a contradiction in intention (unlimited in total, scarce per period) but it is stated as two separate bullets with no reconciliation, and the models later use a constant annual output w rather than either. Assumption 3 has every participant “obey our regulation unconditionally”, which pre-supposes the regulatory body whose necessity section 5.2 is supposed to argue. 38-40 assumes the statistics are reliable and names the four sources (Our World in Data, Statista, World Inequality Database, CEIC). 41-42 assumes mining follows “basic priciples of economics”, 43 that activities are “stable and predictable” so history can estimate parameters (its final clause, “utilize histical data to predict some unknow parameters”, is glued to the notation table inside block 44 and is therefore carried by the next chapter). Every bullet removes a degree of freedom rather than bounding it, so limit throughout.

heading: 3 Notations
note: 1 block, 49 words. Block 44 opens with the last clause of assumption 6 (“utilize histical data to predict some unknow parameters”) and then runs straight into the table and the heading, so the chapter shares a block with the previous chapter; the table itself reads: q output of minerals (kg), p price (dollar/kg), delta market share (%), pi profit (billion dollars), C cost of mining, k capital input, l labour input (thousand persons). Only seven symbols are defined, and the ones the model actually solves with — alpha, beta, A, Q, v, w, the upper bounds delta^U, k^U, l^U — are absent; block 45 says “specific value of those parameters will be given later” and slides straight into “4 Global Equity Model 4.1 Dimensions of Global Equity”.

heading: 4 Global Equity Model / 4.1 Dimensions of Global Equity
note: 13 measured blocks, 165 words, four printed units. 46-54 is a single sentence destroyed by the column/line breaker into nine fragments — “When it comes to equity, it refers to the equity between people in different social status, the equity between rich and poor countries, the equity between the present and the future generations … Global equity is the quality of being globally fair considering natural resources, economy, health & education, environment and life quality, which considers need and justice.” That sentence is the paper's formal definition, and its five named dimensions are exactly the HELEN acronym, so the definition and the indicator system are the same act. 55 names the five dimensions and their initials (H, E, L, E, N) — note that Economy and Environment share the letter E, so the acronym is ambiguous in writing. 56-57 is the diagram statement plus caption: “five fist-level indicators and sixteen second-level indicators” with “Figure 2: Diagram of HELEN Model”. The count of sixteen is only recoverable by adding the sub-sections later (4 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 3), because the paper never prints the indicator list as a table — Table 1 in this paper belongs to the market model, not the equity model.

heading: 4.2 HELEN Model (4.2.1 Natural Resources, 4.2.2 Economic, 4.2.3 Life Quality, 4.2.4 Environmental, 4.2.5 Health & Education)
note: 60 measured blocks, 819 words, 34 printed units — a taxonomy, not prose: every indicator gets a numbered label and a one- or two-line gloss, and the line breaker split the glosses, so the group boundaries follow the labels rather than the blocks. Natural resources (58-73) has four indexes: PDI, the rank correlation between production and demand, where “the closer the correlation coefficient is to 1, the fairer the allocation”; IOI, the coefficient of variation of imports and exports; and two concentration indexes, HHIRO for occupancy and HHIRC for consumption, both of them Hirschman-Herfindahl sums of squared country shares. The HHI formula in 66 is printed correctly (sum of S_i^2) but the text before it calls HHI “a comprehensive index to measure industrial concentration” and then applies it to resource occupancy, which is an analogy, not a derivation. Economy (74-80) uses Gini of wealth per capita and Theil of GDP per capita; life quality (81-94) uses Moran's I, the only place where a real derivation appears (81-85), applied to PPI, poverty share and urban population ratio; environment (95-105) uses four Moran indexes (carbon, effluent, solid waste, pollution-control investment); health and education (106-117) uses coefficients of variation of compulsory-education completion, infant mortality and access to health resources, the last built as the average of three sub-indicators. Two structural observations: every index is a *dispersion* measure (rank correlation, CV, HHI, Moran, Gini, Theil), so a high HELEN score means countries are similar, not that they are well off — the same property as the GE definition in the other 2022 papers, and it is never stated; and six of the fourteen indicators are Moran indexes whose weights depend on a contiguity matrix that is never printed or tested for sensitivity.

heading: 4.3 Weight of Index (4.3.1 AHP, 4.3.2 EWM, 4.3.3 comprehensive weights and composite score)
note: 19 blocks, 468 words. 118 is the provenance and the sample: all indexes computed for 2001-2020, “including almost all the countries around the world”, sourced from Statista. 119 commits to the AHP + EWM combination. AHP (120-124) is a pair-comparison matrix whose entries are never printed, the geometric-mean weight formula, normalisation, and a consistency test reported only as “CI = 0.0593 < 0.1” — the consistency ratio needs CI/RI and RI depends on the matrix order, which is not given, so the pass is not checkable. EWM (125-130) is the standard chain p_ij, e_j, d_j = 1 - e_j, psi_j, printed correctly with equation numbers (2)-(5). 131-134 gives the comprehensive weight omega_ij = omega_i omega_j|i and the composite score I = sum_i sum_j V_ij omega_ij; equation (7) is written with the outer sum running “i = 1 … 4” while HELEN has five first-level dimensions, a count slip in the printed formula. 135-136 pushes the actual weights into “Figure 3: Weight of Index”, so no weight is ever printed as a number — every downstream score in the paper depends on a figure the text does not quantify.

heading: 4.4 Validation
note: 3 blocks, 121 words. 137 applies the model by region (North America, Latin America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania) and glues two captions, “Figure 4: Piketty's Index” and “Figure 5: Global equity Index”, into the same block. 138 introduces the external benchmark: Piketty's top-10% national income share, which is background for the comparison rather than a result. 139 is the comparison itself: “The result of two indexes show a high degree of consistency. Europe and Oceania have the lowest levels of inequity. Africa and Latin America have the highest levels of inequity. Equity index of Asia is higher than Europe and lower than Africa.” This is a rank-ordering comparison across six regions with no correlation coefficient, no table and no number — the validation is qualitative and rests on the reader seeing two figures side by side. It is also the paper's only external validation of the equity model; there is no held-out period, no second data source and no error metric.

heading: 5 Asteroid Mining Market Model / 5.1 Factor Market (5.1.1 Participants, 5.1.2 Clustering, 5.1.3 Result, 5.1.4 Production Function)
note: 35 measured blocks, 852 words, 16 printed units. 140-141 is the model overview with the Figure 6 caption. 142 is the most important scope sentence in the paper and is easy to miss: “we only discuss the change of IOI, MIPPI snd TIGDP, regarding other indexes as invariant” — of the sixteen HELEN indicators only three are perturbed by the mining market, so the equity impact reported in 5.4 is a three-indicator effect. 143-150 defines the factor-market participants: government agencies (main producer early, then capital provider) and research institutions (talent, innovation). 151-154 builds the country-capability metric from three observables (papers in the space field, space-industry employees, market value of listed space companies) — proxies for technology, talent and capital, chosen without any citation. 155 fixes the sample at “the countries with mining capacity (20 countries)”. 156-164 is the method chain: KPCA for visualisation because three dimensions cannot be plotted, then system clustering with Ward connectivity into four clusters; 164 cites Appendix A for the algorithm. 165 says the countries fall into “41 categories”, which contradicts both 164 (“four clusters”) and the five-item list that follows; the footnote inside 166 explains the fifth class as countries without mining capacity, so the intended number is five and “41” is a typo. The list is the paper's own capability ranking: Leader (US, EU), Advancer (China, Russia, India), Pursuer (Israel, South Korea, Japan, Iran, UAE), Outsider (Mexico, Australia, Brazil, Egypt, New Zealand, Indonesia, Thailand, Saudi Arabia), Others. 172 prints Figure 7 and Figure 8. 173-174 builds the production side: q_i = A_i k_i^alpha l_i^beta with alpha = 0.3 and beta = 0.7 taken from Nicholson [6] for all countries, while A_i is estimated per cluster “use its historical mineral data for regression analysis … take one country in each category” — Appendix B gives the log-linear estimator. A single representative country therefore sets the technology level for its entire cluster.

heading: 5.2 Production Side of Asteroid Mining (5.2.1 Participant, 5.2.2 Upper bound of market share, 5.2.3 Cost-benefit, 5.2.4 Equilibrium)
note: 48 measured blocks, 1016 words, 21 printed units, the densest chapter in the paper. 175 maps the production side onto participants and relationships. 176 states the causal claim that justifies the whole regulatory layer — “It is clearly not enough just relying on the sense of responsibility of developed countries to maintain equity, so the intervention of the international regulatory organization is indispensable” — and 177 supplies the legal basis from the Moon Agreement (“due regard shall be paid to the interest of present and future generations”), which is background quoted to license the institution. 178-185 lists the four responsibilities of the regulator: keep an information registry, set and enforce upper bounds on market share, review mining requests, supervise and fine violations. These are model constraints, so define. 186-187 defines the bound as need: each country's resource gap, “the difference between consumption and production, or $0 if production is greater than consumption”. 188-198 is the factor-analysis machine that turns the gap into needs: latent variable model X = AZ + eps, Sigma_x = AA^T + Sigma_eps, factor scores Z-hat = A^T R_x^{-1} X, and contribution weights lambda_j / sum lambda_i. 199-213 is the cost-benefit core: profit pi_i = Revenue_i - Cost_i, inverse demand p(Q) = 12016.08 - 30.18Q fitted on world nickel production and price (Appendix B), conditional factor demands, and the minimised cost C_i = q^{1/(alpha+beta)} B_i v^{alpha/(alpha+beta)} w^{beta/(alpha+beta)}. 214-222 closes with the Cournot problem: the two-player case, then the constrained program max p(Q)q_i - C_i(q_i) subject to Q <= delta^U, k_i <= k^U_i, l_i <= l^U_i for i = 1..n, with Figure 9 for the process. 222 prints the equilibrium market shares: Leader 53.20%, Advancer 26.13%, Pursuer 15.22%, Outsider 5.16%, Others 0.0%. Those five numbers are the hinge of every later result, and they are produced by a program whose alpha = 0.3, beta = 0.7 are borrowed constants, whose A_i comes from one representative country per cluster, and whose demand curve comes from terrestrial nickel — three transfers that are not validated anywhere.

heading: 5.3 Product Market of Asteroid Mining (5.3.1 Distribution, 5.3.2 Economy, 5.3.3 Natural Resources, 5.3.4 Life Quality) / 5.4 Impact on Global Equity
note: 35 measured blocks, 876 words, 17 printed units. 223-224 is the 5.3 heading and 5.3.1. 225 argues the benefit distribution mode (miners own what they extract and may resell, and because the regulator caps volume “there won't be large-scale monopoly and profiteering”), which is the paper's assumption about property rights, not a result. 226-236 lists who profits: miners as owners, sponsors via dividends with “at least ten to fifteen years from project funding to successful profitability”, processors because asteroid ore has low purity, and the wider supply chain. 237-240 derives the GDP channel GDP^a_i = GDP^b_i + delta_i Q P(Q), 241-242 prints Table 2 with the change rates: Leader +1.54%, Advancer +0.68%, Pursuer +0.04%, Outsider +0.01%, Others 0.00% — a monotone decay in exactly the market-share order of 222, which is what the formula mechanically delivers. 243 states the scarcity-relief mechanism; 244-245 derives the dependence index DI^a_i = DI^b_i + delta_i Q / TC_i and 246-247 prints Table 3: Leader -72.96%, Advancer -22.64%, Pursuer +1.03%, Outsider +12.96%, Others +13.42% — a sign reversal worth noting, because the three weakest classes become *more* import-dependent as the leaders substitute asteroid supply for trade. 248-255 does the same for prices with PPI, Table 4: -2.41%, -0.65%, -0.11%, -0.01%, 0%. 256 applies HELEN to the three changed indicators only and gives partial figures (0.725, 0.445 appear in the block, the rest is elided). 257 gives the headline: “Global Equity raises from 0.525 to 0.579 after asteroid mining.” Two cautions: the movement is +0.054 and is never tested against the weight uncertainty of Figure 3, and the sign of the equity change depends on the three chosen indicators — 5.4 is silent about the six Moran indicators and the four resources indexes that 142 declared invariant.

heading: 6 Model Adjustment (6.1 Changes of conditions, 6.2 Impact on mining patterns, 6.3 Impact of changes in national power)
note: 17 blocks, 831 words, 14 printed units. 258 poses the participant change (states give way to private firms), 259 imports Infant Industry Theory as the mechanism, and 260 spells out the subsidy path (high subsidies early, tapering as the industry matures) — the only place where a change is given an explicit causal driver. 261-262 sets the regulatory scenario: the same market with the market-share cap removed, compared against the capped case. 263 leaves the national-power change as a promise (“we will conduct quantitative analysis accordingly”) that is discharged only through SEM in 6.3. 264-267 is the model adjustment: both changes at once, the number of firms per country estimated from the current count of space companies, and the two regulatory cases — “the upper bound of market share is fixed at 30%. And for the second, the market share is not limited”. 268 prints Figures 11 and 12 and the intuition (the response curve steepens for the leader and flattens for the followers), 269-271 states the shift formally: “q'_1 > q_2 / q_1 q'_2”, which is the paper's most garbled line — the intended statement is q'_1/q'_2 > q_1/q_2, i.e. the output distribution becomes more unbalanced, and the printed fragments do not say it. 272 reports the simulation in 186 words: with more firms the equity index first rises, then falls, then flattens — and the explanation given is that early entrants are advanced-country firms earning monopoly profit, until technology spreads. 273 states the trade-off: “the restriction on market share can indeed better maintain global equity, but it also has its cost”, and the number attached to the cost is the enterprise count at which equity turns, “at 1200”. 274 opens 6.3. Note the restriction is being judged on a simulated curve whose own turning point (1200 firms) is far outside the observed count of space companies, so the cost statement is an extrapolation. Section 6.3 (SEM) is the single 96-word paragraph block 275; it sits at the head of the next coded chapter because its own text runs into the “Royalties” heading.

heading: 7 Policy Proposal (7.1 Collect Royalties, 7.2 Strict Approval Procedures, 7.3 Encourage cooperative development)
note: 31 measured blocks, 989 words, 15 printed units; block 275's tail carries the “Royalties” heading, so the chapter starts inside the SEM block and the block stays with the policy chapter for its heading. 276-277 is the legal background: the 2015 US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, the dispute over whether it violates the Outer Space Treaty, and the counter-argument from the Moon Treaty and the Law of the Sea that celestial bodies are “the common heritage of mankind” and therefore royalties are legitimate. 278-289 is policy 7.1 in three numbered parts: resources held privately but subject to royalties, a progressive fee keyed to the value of the claimed resources with a common threshold and rate; royalties paid into an international fund distributed to citizens with a bias to least developed countries; and part of the fund used for concessional loans to build space capability. 290 is the trade-off assessment and the sharpest paragraph in the chapter: royalties are “a more moderate public policy than upper bound on market share … it avoids rigid uniformity, and still reserves some development space for developed countries”, i.e. the policy is preferred because it is softer on the incumbents that the model showed capturing 53% of output. 291-302 is 7.2, strict approval with five review criteria (volume and value, space pollution, equipment deployed, applicant integrity, heritage destruction). 303-304 explains the transmission (approval -> price stability -> equilibrium shift -> equity via SEM) and 305 is 7.3, cooperation with royalty reductions as the incentive. Every recommendation is addressed to “the international regulatory organization”, an institution that does not exist and whose creation the paper does not propose; the feasibility discussion the abstract promises is compressed into single trade-off sentences in 290 and 273.

heading: 8 Sensitivity Analysis
note: 4 blocks, 132 words, three printed units. 306-307 fixes the parameter: the market-share cap delta^U, swept over 0.26, 0.28, 0.30, 0.32 and 0.34, with the equity index plotted against the number of companies; 308 is that plot, “Figure 14: Sensitivity Analysis”. 309 is the verdict: “for every chosen delta^U … global equity index has the same trend as the third question. The result shows the stability of our model.” This is a one-parameter, shape-only test: no score, no turning point and no rank change is reported for any delta^U, so the claim is that five curves look alike, and the ±0.04 range around the 0.30 baseline is narrow relative to the 0.525-0.579 movement the model is being used to argue about. The parameters that actually drive the results — alpha and beta (0.3/0.7), the fitted demand intercept and slope (12016.08, 30.18), the three capability proxies in 151-154 and the A_i of each cluster — are never perturbed. Block 309's tail glues “9 Strength and Weakness 9.1 Strength”.

heading: 9 Strength and Weakness (9.1 Strength, 9.2 Weakness)
note: 5 blocks, 247 words, five printed units, the shortest evaluation chapter in this batch. Three strengths, all self-assessments: the indicator selection is “scientific and comprehensive” because it drew on “over 20 sets of data from over 180 countries” (310); the AHP + EWM pairing balances judgement against data (311); and data processing used random-forest interpolation, unit unification and country-code merging (312). The third is the one that matters, because no earlier section describes random-forest interpolation — section 3.2 of the assumptions lists only data sources, and the paper never says how missing values were handled, so the strength claim describes a procedure the body never reports. The two weaknesses are real: no sudden-impact factors, justified by restating assumption 6 rather than by testing, and a high data demand with “Moran Index … rather difficult to calculate”. There is no conclusion chapter and no third limitation section: block 314's tail glues “References”, and the reference list 315-323 (fifteen entries, mostly law and space-policy sources) plus Appendix A and Appendix B (324-330) are not coded. Appendix B does hold the only reproducibility material in the paper — the log-linear estimator for A and the nickel-data regression that produced p(Q) = 12016.08 - 30.18Q.
